title: AI, Kids & School
hook: Banning AI is like banning calculators — futile and beside the point. The real job is teaching kids to use it honestly, to learn with it, and to know when it's lying.
key_points: Using AI to learn is great; using it to skip learning defeats the purpose.
Schools differ widely — know your school's rules before using it for work.
Teach the skills AI can't replace: judgment, verifying, and original thinking.
Mind age limits and privacy: many AI tools aren't built for young children.
content_html: AI has thrown schools into a genuine scramble, and the instinct to simply ban it is understandable but mostly doomed — the tools are everywhere, and pretending otherwise just drives use underground. The more useful frame is the one we eventually reached with calculators and the internet: the technology isn't going away, so the task is teaching kids to use it well. And "well" has a clear dividing line. Using AI to learn — to explain a hard concept, quiz yourself, or get unstuck — is wonderful. Using it to skip learning — pasting in an essay prompt and handing in the output — defeats the entire point of the assignment, which was to build the skill in your own head.
extra_html: A few practical notes for families. School policies vary enormously and are changing fast, so the first move is always to know the specific rules for a class before using AI on its work; honest disclosure beats getting caught. The skills worth nurturing are exactly the ones AI can't do for you: judgment, checking whether an answer is actually true, and thinking of something original. It's also worth treating AI as a fallible tutor with kids — a great moment to teach that even confident-sounding answers need verifying. Finally, mind the practicalities: many AI products have age limits and weren't designed for young children, and kids should learn early not to share personal details with a chatbot. Used thoughtfully, AI can be one of the best learning aids ever invented; used lazily, it quietly robs the learning it was supposed to support.

related.title: AI as a Tutor
related.hook: A chatbot is a tutor with infinite patience: ask it to explain anything five different ways at any level, with no judgment. Just remember it can be confidently wrong.

related.title: Using AI Responsibly
related.hook: The point of AI literacy isn't to use AI for everything — it's to use it well: check its work, be honest that you used it, and know the moments to put it down.

related.title: Your Data & Privacy
related.hook: When you type into a free AI tool, you might be the product. What you share can be stored, reviewed by humans, and used to train future models — so share like it's not private.

flashcards.prompt: What's the key distinction for students using AI?

choices.text: Using it to learn (good) vs. using it to skip learning (self-defeating)
Using it on weekdays vs. weekends

flashcards.explanation_html: AI as a tutor or study aid builds understanding; copying its answers to avoid the work skips the learning the assignment was meant to create.

flashcards.prompt: Before a student uses AI on schoolwork, what should they check?
flashcards.back_html: Their school or teacher's specific policy — rules vary a lot, and what counts as allowed help in one class is cheating in another.
